The thesis that mathematical objects possess a form of objectivity independent of human psychological or social construction finds strong support in several interconnected lines of reasoning. The indispensability argument establishes that our best scientific theories quantify over mathematical entities and are confirmed by the empirical success of those theories; the scientific realist who accepts electrons on the basis of theoretical indispensability has no principled grounds for rejecting the existence of mathematical objects on similar grounds.
This commitment to mathematical realism aligns seamlessly with the lived experience of mathematical practice itself. The phenomenology of mathematical discovery, in which mathematicians encounter unexpected theorems, failed proofs corrected by necessity rather than convention, and surprising connections across independently developed branches, is more naturally described as exploration of a domain with determinate structure than as invention of arbitrary formal systems. Such experiences reveal a resistance and autonomy in mathematical reality that cannot be adequately captured by appeals to mere human creativity or agreement, pointing instead to an objective realm that mathematicians investigate much as empirical scientists probe the physical world.
Nominalist alternatives that attempt to eliminate mathematical objects in favor of physical inscriptions or mental constructions face decisive technical objections, as they either fail to recover the full expressive power of standard mathematics or generate circularity by presupposing mathematical structure in the account meant to eliminate it. These shortcomings underscore the robustness of the realist position, affirming that mathematical objects exist with an independence that transcends human invention.
